en: Points added to your driving licence after certain traffic offences.
A document that proves your vehicle has valid insurance cover.
A declaration that a vehicle is kept off public roads and is not taxed for road use.
Extra pedals for the supervisor or instructor to help control the car.
A driving teacher officially approved to give paid lessons (ADI in the UK).
A service that helps if your vehicle stops working on the road.
The UK road tax (VED) you must pay to use a vehicle on public roads.
The unique identification number stamped on the vehicle's frame.
Paying UK vehicle tax (VED) so the vehicle can be used on public roads.
A learner driving licence that allows practice driving under set restrictions before a full licence.
A lane that is open for normal moving traffic (not closed or for emergency use only).
A marked bay beside a motorway for stopping in an emergency when there is no hard shoulder.
Both indicators flashing together to warn other drivers of a hazard or sudden slowing.
Pulling a trailer attached behind your vehicle.
A one-wheeled passenger compartment fixed to the side of a motorcycle.
When one or more lanes are temporarily closed, often due to roadworks or an incident.
A flat tyre caused by a hole that lets the air out.
When a vehicle stops working and can no longer be driven normally.
Posts with decreasing bars (3, 2, 1) showing how close you are to a motorway exit.
When vehicles pack closely together, often causing sudden braking waves.
Temporary speed limits shown on overhead signs that change with traffic conditions.
A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
A free roadside phone on motorways that connects you to operators who can send help.
Small roadside posts that show distance markers and the direction to the nearest emergency phone.
Small electric vehicles for people with limited mobility, usually for pavements and short trips.
A motorway services site with parking, fuel, and facilities where you can stop safely to rest.
A free phone fixed beside the motorway that links you to help and shows your location.
Raised reflective road markers that help show where lanes and edges are, especially at night.
A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
Specialist road staff who manage incidents and traffic on motorways and major A-roads.
An extra uphill lane for slow vehicles so faster traffic is not held up.
A part of the road marked for cyclists, shown by a bicycle symbol and lane lines.
The top of a hill where your view of the road ahead is often limited.
Towns or villages with buildings close to the road; a 30 mph limit often applies with street lights.
Widened spots on a narrow road where vehicles can pull in to let others pass.
A junction where roads meet with no give-way or stop signs or road markings.
A lane reserved for buses (and sometimes taxis/cycles) during the times shown on signs.
Flashing lights on a vehicle used to show you intend to turn or change lane.
A town or village area with buildings beside the road; street lighting often marks a 30 mph zone.
A controlled driving movement such as reversing, turning, or parking.
Lenses that are darkened or coloured, reducing how much light reaches your eyes.
Using indicators (or other signals) to show other road users what you intend to do.
A bridge where the road is too narrow for two vehicles to pass easily side by side.
Feeling sleepy or half-asleep, so your reactions and attention are reduced.
Blocks or gets in the way of other traffic so it cannot pass freely.
A large goods truck used to carry heavy loads (UK term for a truck).
Sleepiness that slows your thinking and reactions while driving.
Bright reflective strips or panels that help others see a vehicle, especially in the dark.
Big trucks that carry freight; often called LGVs in the UK.
Temporary signs that send traffic along a different route around a closure or roadworks.
Road features such as humps or narrowings designed to keep vehicle speeds lower.
High-speed roads with controlled access for most traffic, shown by blue signs in the UK.
A place where roads meet or cross, such as a T-junction or crossroads.
When you cannot see far enough ahead because something blocks your view.
The raised stone or concrete edge between the road and the pavement.
Roads in housing areas where people live, often with parked cars and pedestrians.
Large trucks that carry freight; often called HGVs in the UK.
Paths for people walking, usually beside a road (pavements/sidewalks).
Something blocking the road so traffic cannot pass freely.
Parked beside another parked vehicle, blocking a lane or space.
Driving after drinking alcohol or taking drugs that impair your ability to drive.
Vehicle Excise Duty — the UK government charge for using a vehicle on public roads.
Suddenly changing direction, often to avoid something in the road.
Getting off a bicycle (or motorcycle) to walk beside it.
Extreme tiredness that reduces concentration and safe driving ability.
Being fully awake and ready to notice hazards and react quickly.
Pressing the accelerator hard in an automatic car so it changes to a lower gear for quicker acceleration.
To pass a slower vehicle ahead by moving past it into another lane.
When tyres ride up on water and lose grip with the road surface.
Water collecting in low spots on the road after rain.
A person riding a horse on or beside the road; treat them as vulnerable road users.
The gap you leave between your vehicle and the one in front.
Rules that limit where and when you may park, shown by signs or road markings.
Cameras that detect vehicles exceeding the speed limit.
Headlights on their brightest setting; can dazzle others if used wrongly.
Using your direction indicators to show you intend to turn or change lane.
A curve in the road that turns tightly and may need a clear speed reduction.
The parking brake, normally used to hold the vehicle when stopped, not for slowing in motion.
A major road with traffic travelling in opposite directions, separated by a central reservation.
Let other traffic go first when they have priority, instead of continuing ahead of them.
